card_quote: Default disposition (sceptic seed): 'I've heard all this before.' Expects recycled QI material and has complained about errors and missing citations in fact books. / What would register with him: obscure or genuinely disputed cases, sources.
how_read: Read it in order, properly, looking for mistakes, which is how I read these things. Skimmed round 1 because it's QI territory. Got as far as the end of round 8 over a few evenings, hit a page that looked like a practical joke, and didn't feel much need to finish.

w1_friction.note: Unfilled placeholder on the copyright page. Not a promising start.
Drafted with AI. That explains the prose, and it means I'm checking every claim myself.
w1_friction.quote: the entries were drafted with AI tools

w1_friction.note: Newton's apple, Galileo's tower, Einstein's Nobel. I've heard every one of these on QI.
w1_friction.quote: There is an apple in Newton's own account

w1_friction.note: Stukeley's memoir is in the source list, yet the text leans on Britannica for what Newton said. Quote the primary source if you've got it.
w1_friction.quote: according to Encyclopaedia Britannica, traces back to Newton's own later recollection

w1_friction.note: If you're going to make a point of when the compact form appeared, look it up. Saying 'the record does not say' is just admitting you didn't.
w1_friction.quote: The record does not say when the compact form first appeared

w1_friction.note: Same Bloch citation, same Heinlein line, second entry running. Padding.
w1_friction.quote: Arthur Bloch's Murphy's Law Book Two (1980), page 52

w1_friction.note: Stamped TRUE, then the text says he never did it. Duplicate number 31, wrong round header, one Wikipedia cite. Nobody checked this page.
w1_friction.quote: Franklin never flew a kite in a thunderstorm

w1_friction.note: As I remember it, Priestley's account has Franklin flying the kite and drawing sparks from the key, no lightning strike. 'Invented later' is the overcorrection the book warns about on page 20.
w1_friction.quote: the dramatic scene around it is not on the record

w1_friction.note: A whole entry resting on a single Wikipedia article. That's the 'citation needed' problem with a citation stuck on it.
'The record makes plain.' Which record? Every page appeals to this unnamed authority instead of just citing the thing.
w1_friction.quote: The odd name stuck for a reason the record makes plain

w1_friction.note: Debunks equal transit time and then won't say why the upper air speeds up. Mention circulation or the Coanda argument, or don't open the box.
w1_friction.quote: The record does not say why the upper air speeds up

w1_friction.note: Odd thing to print. Reads like a note the writer left for himself.
Someone's having a laugh. Written in parody journal-speak and sourced to 'various laboratory studies'. That's where I put it down.

w1_best.why: Didn't know about the 2026 Dawson and de Meza reanalysis. Genuinely disputed, properly cited, and it cuts against the smug pop version.
Didn't know the 1913 Monte Carlo run traces to a 1959 Huff book. That's new, and it's sourced to page numbers.
Yerkes-Dodson being forty mice and Hebb's later curve. Good, and fairly obscure.
Levitt and List on Hawthorne is one I knew, but it's done well.
Newcomb's worn log tables, and the note about election misuse is sensible.

w1_flat.why: The most tired myth in existence.
Einstein's Nobel for the photoelectric effect is a pub quiz staple.
Contradicts its own verdict and probably overcorrects the history.
A parody page with no source. Embarrassing.
Raises the lift question and then ducks it.

w1_review.headline: Better sourced than QI, and then it falls over twice
w1_review.body: Credit where due: most entries cite actual papers, and a handful (Dunning-Kruger's 2026 reanalysis, the Monte Carlo run, Yerkes-Dodson) told me something I didn't know. But round 1 is recycled QI, the prose is a template that leans on 'the record' instead of citing it, several stories are just told twice, and there are two pages, a Franklin kite entry that contradicts its own verdict and a goldfish page in mock-academic gibberish, that shouldn't be in a book about checking claims. Bottom line: two stars, and I'd tell you to get the Lilienfeld book instead.

w2_review_first: I'd say it's a myth-busting quiz that's better referenced than most, but a lot of it is stuff any QI viewer already knows. And for a book whose whole point is checking claims, it has a couple of pages that are plainly wrong or plainly unchecked, which rather undermines the premise.

w2_lost.why: Round 1. Archimedes, Newton, Galileo, Einstein. I skimmed the lot.
The physics round, Coriolis and the sink. I've given this lecture at the pub myself.
Round 8 felt like a list of management slogans rather than myths.
The goldfish page. That's where I stopped taking it seriously and stopped reading.

w2_read_aloud.why: The run of 26 blacks is something everyone's heard, and finding it starts in a 1959 book is a nice reveal.
Six downloads, two by her own lawyers. Hard to beat.
Tailless rats breeding. Grimly funny and well sourced.
Muphry's law, with the Economist pasty. Would go down well with anyone who's ever corrected someone online.
Proper physics about toast. Good one to make people guess wrong.

w2_cut.why: The sink myth has been debunked on every science programme for thirty years.

w2_book2: One more page stamped with a verdict its own text contradicts.
